notes.meaning: Once the judge Ehud was gone, the people of Israel turned away from God again. Without a godly leader to hold them accountable, they slipped back into idol worship during a long season of peace.

Because Israel abandoned God, He allowed Jabin, a Canaanite king ruling from Hazor, to conquer and control them. This enemy was not an invader from far away, but from the very people Israel had failed to drive out years before. Sisera commanded Jabin's army from Harosheth-hagoyim.

Jabin crushed the Israelites with cruel treatment for twenty long years, backed by nine hundred terrifying iron war chariots. Finally broken by this heavy burden, the people cried out to the Lord for rescue.
At that time, God gave leadership to Deborah, a prophetess and the wife of Lappidoth. As a prophetess, she heard from the Spirit of God and taught His will to the people.

differ.view: Deborah's leadership was maternal, and she took care to respect and support male leadership by calling Barak to command the army rather than taking the military role herself.
Deborah serves as a biblical model showing that the Holy Spirit freely gives prophetic and leadership gifts to women in the life of God's people.

notes.meaning: Deborah held open court under a well-known palm tree in the hills of Ephraim. The people of Israel traveled there to have her settle disputes and guide them back to God's laws.
Deborah sent for a warrior named Barak and delivered God's direct order to him. He was told to gather ten thousand men from the northern tribes of Naphtali and Zebulun and march them up Mount Tabor.
The Lord promised that He would draw Sisera, with all his troops and iron chariots, out to the Kishon River. There, God Himself would hand Sisera over to Barak for defeat.
Barak refused to go to battle unless Deborah went with him. He wanted the prophetess by his side as a living sign of God's presence, guidance, and blessing in the fight.
Deborah agreed to go, but warned Barak that his hesitation meant he would not receive the personal honor for the victory. Instead, the Lord would hand Sisera over to a woman.
Barak mustered ten thousand foot soldiers from the tribes of Zebulun and Naphtali at Kedesh. Deborah marched alongside him, giving the volunteer soldiers confidence for the coming battle.

This brief note explains that Heber the Kenite had split off from his relatives, who were related to Moses by marriage, and set up camp near Kedesh. His family's location becomes essential to how the battle ends.

When Sisera learned that Barak had gathered an army on Mount Tabor, he called up his entire strike force. He brought out all nine hundred iron chariots and his whole army to the Kishon River, expecting an easy victory on the flat ground.

Deborah told Barak that the appointed day of victory had arrived and that the Lord Himself was marching out ahead of them. Trusting God's promise, Barak led his ten thousand foot soldiers down the mountain straight toward the dreaded chariots.

The Lord threw Sisera's army and chariots into sudden terror and confusion before Barak's advancing troops. Seeing his powerful force collapse, Sisera jumped down from his chariot and ran away on foot.
Barak chased the fleeing chariots and troops all the way back to their base at Harosheth-hagoyim. The entire Canaanite army was wiped out by the sword, leaving not a single soldier alive.
While the battle raged, Sisera fled on foot toward the tent of Jael, the wife of Heber the Kenite. He thought he would be safe there because King Jabin had a peace agreement with Heber's household.
Jael stepped outside to meet Sisera, invited him into her private tent, and told him not to be afraid. She then covered the exhausted general with a rug to keep him warm and hidden.
Sisera asked for a little water because of his burning thirst, but Jael gave him a bowl of milk instead. This friendly act quenched his thirst, helped him feel secure, and made him sleepy.
Sisera told Jael to guard the doorway of the tent and deny that anyone was inside if searchers came by. He counted on the strict privacy of a woman's tent to keep pursuers from checking inside.

While Sisera was in a deep sleep from total exhaustion, Jael quietly approached him with a wooden tent peg and a hammer. She struck the peg through his temple into the ground, killing him on the spot.

differ.view: Jael's use of deceit is understandable because wartime suspends normal rules of hospitality, and her loyalty was to God and His oppressed people above all else.
Jael's act violated the sacred laws of hospitality, good faith, and truthfulness, so her deception and killing cannot be morally defended as a godly example.
Sisera represents the power of sin, teaching believers that sin must not merely be fought or held back, but completely put to death.

notes.meaning: When Barak arrived in pursuit, Jael came out and showed him the fallen general lying dead with the tent peg through his temple. In this striking way, Deborah's prophecy came true: the final glory of defeating Sisera belonged to a woman.

That day, God broke the power of King Jabin before the children of Israel. The Israelites kept pressing their advantage in the years that followed until Jabin and his kingdom were completely destroyed.
